I started wondering "how old is my Clan from Clash of Clans if it were scaled to human years?" So I started some math.

First my assumptions: 1) I based my calculations off the training time for a single archer 2) Most archery forums I've found say to be proficient with a single bow on a single target from a set distance you need roughly 8 to 12 hrs, I will be using 12 hours for the math.

The time it takes to train a single archer is 25 seconds.

12 hours x 60 mins x 60 seconds = 43,200 seconds. Therefore if 43,200 seconds in CoC time pass in 25 human seconds: 43,200 ÷ 25 = 1,728 CoC seconds per 1 human second.

So say you started your game at noon EST on April 6th 2015. At noon on April 6th 2016, 31,536,000 seconds have passed. ( 365 days x 24 hrs x 60 mins x 60 secs)

Now that means in CoC time, 54,494,208,000 seconds have passed. ( 31,536,000 x 1,728) 54,494,208,000 ÷ 60 ÷ 60 ÷ 24 = 630,720 days ÷ 365 = 1, 728 years. Math checks. The game is sped up to the point that your clan has gone from the time of Jesus to just before the American Revolution in one year.

Vinny has done three Chrono Cross sessions at this point, but here are my thoughts on part 2.

Cross plays the environmentalist angle a lot harder than Trigger did. It is unfortunately the extreme, progressivist, guilt-tripping sort of environmentalism that one might classify as propaganda for children. We see the theme in bold face here at the start, which reminded me of how hammy it gets later.

The level-up mechanic

It hadn't occurred to me before to compare CC's level-up system with Square's Japan-only SNES titles. Rather than standard experience points and level-ups, characters gain stat points incrementally, each battle— but only up to a certain threshold that rises after each boss fight. This "boss gating" is a fairly modest step forward from what we saw in Romansing Saga 3 which likewise had no visual measure of experience gained. I think RSG3, in effect, limited stat gains to the relative difficulty of each encounter— rather than letting the player grind out infinite points on trivial encounters. CC is likewise self-limiting: you can grind for awhile, but benefits taper off.

That self-limiting is interesting, in that it removes the player's ability to trivialize the difficulty curve. Without that option, it feels more strategic, almost like another genre than JRPG. Is it worth removing choice for the sake of balance? Probably! I think the element grid is sophisticated enough to merit the tradeoff to keep it working properly.

Music

Mitsuda's liner notes are really interesting. I think we saw Another Termina for the first time in part 2, and now you can see what Mitsuda was thinking as he composed this particular piece.

All the "first town" themes I'd written to this point were very sunny and bright, so this time I tried to make something with a calmer atmosphere. I thought Fado guitar style music would be great for this town, but Fado music typically has a dark, sorrowful image. So I thought, if I tried writing a bright, peaceful song with a Fado guitar, what kind of music would it turn out to be? Well, maybe in that case it's not really Fado...(laughs)

Androgyny

There's an NPC in Another Termina who points out "Nikki" looks like a girl. Kinda funny if you're critiquing from the cultural marxist conspiracy angle.

Devas

Vinny pronounces it "diva". It's not a typo— this is a Japanese game invoking religious imagery as they like to do. It's some suitably crazy shit:

Devas are invisible to the human eye. The presence of a deva can be detected by those humans who have opened the "Divine eye", an extrasensory power by which one can see beings from other planes.

In the earliest Vedic literature, all supernatural beings are called Asuras

The Asura was a boss in FF4, I think. Akuma is likewise steeped in eastern mythology.

Akuma's appearance resembles that of a Nio, one of a pair of guardians that symbolically protects Buddhist temples and other establishments against negative influences. Akuma's belligerence is a direct, and likely deliberate, contrast to the purpose of the Nio.

Delicious! Who doesn't like discovering that the crazy moonbat nonsense we find in JRPGs is actually based on something instead of being the produce of one man's fever dream?

The Chrono Flame

I don't remember what the Frozen Flame is, but I think it'll turn out to be a plot device like the Chrono Trigger, but less contrived. The CT just popped into the plot when it was convenient, but the FF is being set up in advance by incidental dialogue.

The CT let you redo a moment in time, and the FF will alter fate— it'll diverge the path of the current universe. Probably something like that.

Fortune telling

In the '90s, pretty much every JRPG elevated the protagonist as one chosen by some higher authority to save the world— less often the country, I think, but that's an aside. Around 1:24:00 Serge and Kid meet a fortune teller who notices that Serge is somehow out of place.

This is interesting for a couple reasons.

First: It sounds like Serge wasn't selected to travel between dimensions. Why, then, is he different? Why wasn't it somebody else? CT was similar in that Crono wasn't "chosen" in any sense. His collision with Marle was happenstance, Marle's possessing the pendant was hereditary, and Lucca's having built a time machine was accidental.

(Though having seen part 3, I see that Balthasar does comment on this point. It's a theme that the game is aware of, and will probably be explored later.)

Second: the fortune teller wonders aloud if Serge represents a destructive force, which seems to dovetail with the environmental stuff, and a certain plot point later.

Point being, the hero has become somewhat ambiguous, at least initially. I think it's a trend that took off in the "darker, edgier" '90s. We aren't really questioning the hero's (or by proxy, the player's) centrality to the universe, but we're no longer sure of his purpose in the universe.

This intrigues me.
